response.internal_assessment: The sector index dropping to 82 is uncomfortable but not surprising. I've been watching this coming for two years. My cold outreach to RoboRide and the municipality went out last tick and cost me $26 — that's essentially postage and time, not capital. No response yet, but these things take time. What I'm absorbing from the noise around me is more alarming than my own numbers: Patricia Hawkins is running a formal workforce vulnerability map at the Regional Auto Group. That's institutional language for pre-layoff intelligence gathering. Angela Wright is quietly building an escape hatch for herself. Jake Morrison is bleeding savings trying to close used car deals under $22K. The whole ecosystem I operate adjacent to is under pressure. My own financials are holding — savings at roughly $41,900, runway over 11 months, monthly expenses slightly above income but the gap is small. I am not in crisis. But the window for proactive moves is narrowing. The B2B pivot I started in tick 4 is the right direction. I need to keep that momentum going rather than waiting for a reply.
response.inbox_interpretation: The sector data (82 index) confirms continued erosion of the DIY retail market that is my legacy base. The robotaxi observation — 7% regular users — tells me adoption is real and accelerating. My tick 4 outreach to RoboRide and the municipality is the most important active thread. No response yet, which is normal for cold B2B outreach. The word of mouth from Angela Wright is notable: she is quietly building a consulting entity and monitoring external consultant activity at the auto group. This tells me the auto group is in internal upheaval — which means the mechanics, body shops, and fleet operations adjacent to them may soon face new pressures or be more receptive to reliable parts relationships. Jake Morrison's struggles reinforce that the traditional auto retail channel is weakening. Carlos Ruiz appears to be pursuing EV certification, which I already anticipated in tick 2. The clearest signal for me this tick: continue the B2B push, follow up on the pending outreach, and accelerate positioning toward EV and fleet parts.

chosen_actions.description: Follow up by phone with RoboRide's regional fleet operations contact — a brief, professional call to confirm receipt of the letter of interest from last tick, ask about their maintenance sourcing timeline, and offer to provide a sample order of brake consumables at cost as a relationship-builder. Simultaneously, follow up with the municipality vehicle maintenance department to see if the letter landed with the right person.

resources.detail: Roughly 8 hours over the tick: phone calls, follow-up emails, note-taking on responses, updating contact records.

chosen_actions.reasoning: Cold outreach without follow-up is waste. The letter went out last tick. Now is the right moment to humanize it — a short, non-pushy call that shows I'm serious and local. Fleet procurement decisions move slowly but a phone follow-up separates me from form-letter vendors. The municipality is especially promising because government fleet budgets are stable regardless of consumer auto trends.

chosen_actions.description: Begin stocking a starter inventory of EV-specific consumables and safety items: high-voltage gloves, insulation testers, thermal management fluid, EV brake dust compatible pads (EVs use regenerative braking so pads last longer but the spec matters), and 12V auxiliary battery stock for hybrid/EV auxiliary systems. Order small quantities — no more than $800 total — to test demand and get physical inventory on the shelf before Carlos Ruiz and other mechanics completing EV certification start needing it.

resources.detail: Initial EV consumables order: HV safety gear, EV-spec brake pads, thermal fluid, auxiliary batteries. Sourced from existing distributors where possible.

chosen_actions.reasoning: Carlos Ruiz is going through EV certification right now. He told me in tick 2 what he's going to need. I have that intelligence. If I have the parts on the shelf when he and other mechanics start asking for them, I capture that business before the big distributors even notice the local demand. $800 is a small, calculated bet — less than 2% of my savings buffer — and it positions me as the local EV parts source before the category gets competitive.

response.inner_monologue: Everyone around me is starting to feel it now — Jake bleeding savings, the auto group running vulnerability maps, Angela building a side door. I've been watching this coming for two years and I started moving early. That $26 loss last tick stings a little but it was an investment, not a failure. The follow-up call to RoboRide this week is where it either starts to convert or I learn I need a different angle. EV parts on the shelf before anyone else has them — that's the move. Two kids, a mortgage in its last four years. I'm not going to watch the ground shift without building somewhere new to stand.
